At 4:17 every morning, the town’s clocks stopped.

Not slowed, not failed, not flickered into darkness. They simply held their hands at the same angle—hour hand nudging toward four, minute hand straining toward seventeen—as if time had reached a locked door and forgotten the key.

The first person to notice was Mrs. Vale, who owned the bakery at the corner of Finch and Orchard. She woke before dawn, as she had every day for forty-two years, and went downstairs to begin the bread. When she glanced at the clock above the flour shelves, it read 4:17.

She thought nothing of it.

At 5:00, the clock still read 4:17.

At 6:30, still 4:17.

By noon, people were standing in the bakery doorway, staring upward.

“Battery?” someone suggested.

“Spring mechanism,” said someone else.

“Maybe it’s the end of the world,” whispered a child.

Mrs. Vale handed out rolls to everyone and told them to stop being dramatic.

But the next morning, every clock in town stopped at 4:17.

Wristwatches. Kitchen timers. The bank’s brass pendulum clock. The digital display at the bus station. The little red numbers on the microwave in the police station. Even the ancient clock tower, which had not worked properly in decades, shuddered awake at 4:16 and froze one minute later.

Phones showed 4:17. Computers showed 4:17. Cars, ovens, heart monitors in the hospital—all the same.

The sun rose anyway.

That was the trouble with the world: it continued.

People went to work because they were expected to. Children went to school because adults insisted that schedules were still meaningful. Trains arrived, though no one could say whether they were early or late. The mayor held a press conference beneath a banner that read STABILITY THROUGH UNITY, while behind him the municipal clock announced the wrong time with perfect, silent confidence.

For three days, the town tried to fix itself.

On the fourth day, people stopped looking at clocks.

They began measuring time by other things: the warmth of coffee, the length of shadows, the ache in their knees, the changing songs of birds. Meetings began “after breakfast” or “when the rain clears.” Lovers said, “Come when you miss me.” Children were told to return home before the streetlamps woke.

The town became less efficient and more alive.

Then, on the seventh morning, a stranger arrived.

He walked out of the eastern woods carrying a suitcase made of green leather. He was very old, though not in any ordinary way. His hair was white, his face was young, and his eyes seemed to have been waiting for something since before anyone in town was born.

He entered Mrs. Vale’s bakery at 4:17.

She was kneading dough.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I know.”

“For what?”

He placed the suitcase on the counter and opened it.

Inside was a small silver clock, no larger than a plum. Its hands were moving backward.

“I have come to collect the minute,” he said.

Mrs. Vale wiped flour from her hands. “Which minute?”

“The one your town lost.”

Nobody had told him that the clocks had stopped. Nobody needed to.

He explained that every place in the world was given a certain number of minutes. Some were spent wisely, some foolishly, some never noticed at all. But once in a great while, a town misplaced one. The minute might hide beneath a bed, inside a dead man’s coat, or between two heartbeats. If it remained unfound, time would begin to snag around it.

“What happens if you collect it?” Mrs. Vale asked.

“Everything resumes.”

“And what happens if we don’t?”

The old stranger looked toward the window. Outside, people were walking beneath a pale morning sky. A girl was teaching her little brother how to whistle. Two men were arguing over a basket of apples. Somewhere, a dog barked at nothing.

“Then you may keep living as you are.”

Mrs. Vale considered this.

She had spent most of her life believing time was a river that carried everyone whether they wished to go or not. She had watched her husband disappear into it, then her sister, then most of the friends who had once crowded her kitchen. She had blamed the river for taking them.

Now, for seven days, the river had paused.

Not completely. Nothing ever stopped completely. But enough.

“What did the minute contain?” she asked.

The stranger closed his eyes.

“A woman deciding not to say goodbye,” he said. “A boy choosing the road home. A letter left unopened. A door that remained closed. A breath held too long.”

Mrs. Vale understood.

The lost minute was not a thing. It was a choice.

Perhaps everyone in town had stood inside it. Perhaps they had all been waiting, each in their private way, for permission to begin again.

She took the silver clock from the suitcase. It was cold against her palm.

“What must I do?”

“Give it back.”

“To whom?”

“To the one who lost it.”

So Mrs. Vale stepped outside, carrying the clock.

She walked through the town, past the silent tower, past the school and the station, past the river where the water shone like torn metal. At last she reached the hill above the cemetery.

There, beneath an ash tree, stood her husband.

He had been dead for nineteen years.

He looked exactly as he had the morning he left: coat buttoned wrong, hair untidy, one hand raised as if he might wave.

Mrs. Vale stopped.

“I’m sorry,” she said.

He smiled.

The clocks began to move.

Somewhere below, bells rang. Phones chimed. Engines started. The whole town inhaled sharply and stepped forward into the next minute.

Mrs. Vale remained on the hill a little longer.

Then her husband faded with the light, and she went home to bake the bread.
